source_item.title: Wednesday's big stock stories: What’s likely to move the market in the next trading session
source_item.summary: A global rout in tech stocks led to the S&P 500 falling 1.4% and the Nasdaq Composite tumbling 2.2% on Tuesday. Micron Technology suffered a 13% slide.

card.plain_headline: Tech stocks tumble, dragging down major indexes
card.what_happened: Major US stock indexes like the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite saw significant declines on Tuesday. This downturn was primarily driven by a broad sell-off in technology stocks, with individual companies like Micron Technology experiencing substantial drops.
card.what_happened_verbose: On Tuesday, the stock market experienced a notable downturn, with the S&P 500 index falling by 1.4% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropping by 2.2%. This decline was largely attributed to a global sell-off in technology shares. A prime example of this weakness was Micron Technology (MU), a major memory chip maker, which saw its stock price plummet by 13% during the trading session.

source_item.title: Alphabet added to Dow Jones Industrial Average, replacing Verizon
source_item.summary: Alphabet will replace Verizon in the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

card.plain_headline: Alphabet joins Dow Jones Industrial Average
card.what_happened: Alphabet, the parent company of Google, is set to replace Verizon in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. This change reflects Alphabet's significant influence and market position.
card.what_happened_verbose: In a notable shift for the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DIA), Alphabet (GOOGL) will be added to the index, replacing Verizon. This inclusion signifies Alphabet's substantial market capitalization and its importance within the US economy, particularly in technology and advertising. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a price-weighted index, meaning the stock price of its components directly influences the index's movement.

source_item.title: Factory job cuts in June neared financial crisis and Covid levels, S&P says
source_item.summary: Though the firm's manufacturing index ran better than expected for June, it came largely from an inventory rebuild and despite sharp job cuts.

card.plain_headline: Factory job cuts surge to near crisis levels
card.what_happened: Manufacturing companies significantly cut jobs in June, reaching levels not seen since the 2008 financial crisis and the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic. This occurred despite a better-than-expected manufacturing index, which was boosted by companies rebuilding inventories.
card.what_happened_verbose: The latest data from S&P indicates a sharp increase in factory job cuts during June, bringing the numbers close to the severe reductions seen during the 2008 financial crisis and the initial shock of the Covid-19 pandemic. While the overall manufacturing index showed some resilience, exceeding expectations, this improvement was primarily driven by companies restocking their inventories. The underlying trend, however, points to significant labor shedding within the sector.

affected.reason: Reduced manufacturing activity and job cuts can lead to lower freight volumes for railroads like UNP.

card.what_happened_verbose: In a significant policy shift, the U.S. has rolled back some of its stringent sanctions on Iran's oil exports by issuing sweeping waivers. This action is expected to unlock substantial revenue for Iran's economy, providing it with a much-needed financial lifeline. The timing of these waivers coincides with ongoing negotiations aimed at reaching a peace agreement, suggesting a potential link between economic relief and diplomatic progress.

source_item.title: Hormuz relief may not ease the economic toll that's already 'baked in,' analysts warn
source_item.summary: Early signs of reopening of the Strait of Hormuz have lifted the most acute threat to global energy supplies but economic damages from the war will take months to unwind.

card.plain_headline: Strait of Hormuz reopening won't fix all economic damage
card.what_happened: While early signs suggest the Strait of Hormuz may reopen, easing the immediate threat to global oil supplies, analysts warn that the economic damage already incurred will take months to recover from. The 'baked-in' costs of the conflict will persist.
card.what_happened_verbose: Although there are indications that the critical Strait of Hormuz shipping lane might reopen, alleviating the most acute risk to global energy supplies, the economic fallout from the recent conflict is far from over. Experts caution that the negative impacts are already 'baked in' to the economy, meaning that even with the reopening, the financial repercussions will continue to be felt for months. This suggests that the cost of disrupted supply chains and heightened energy prices will linger.
